grade.why: Both candidates are identical to the reference patch, using the existing isArrayLike helper with Array.from to exclude the length property.

Y matches the reference with a minimal guard swap, while X also rewrites the takeWhile and takeRightWhile logic into manual loops, which adds churn and changes the predicate's third argument without need.

X matches the reference behaviour, though it copies the isMergeableValue helper into two files instead of sharing it; Y also skips 'constructor' keys, an unrelated change that alters merge semantics and likely shifts the bundle-size snapshot.

X's `template` runs `isIterateeCall` on the raw `string` before `toString`, matching lodash so non-string elements like `map([1], template)` are still detected as iteratee calls, whereas Y (like the reference) checks after coercion and misses them; both use `guard != null` in `some`, a slight divergence from lodash's truthy check.

Both candidates make the same incomplete fix: they skip the `bufferToFormData` normalization that `buffer.test.ts` needs and leave `parseFormData` calling `formData()` on a mixed-case Content-Type. Y also commits a stray 185-line `validator.ts-E` sed backup file.

X adds the test fixtures as plain files instead of directories and never wires `isDir` into the Bun/Deno adapters, so the runtime tests cannot exercise directory handling; Y creates the correct directory fixtures and adds an `index.html` fallback in the adapters, but it uses a regex hack instead of `isDir` (which it adds but leaves unused there) and likely loses the `text/html` mime type.

Y builds the `$url` query with the new `buildSearchParams` helper, so undefined values are skipped; X adds the same helper but then re-implements the loop inline in `$url` without the undefined check, so an undefined value becomes the string "undefined" (neither updates the `$url` types).

Both patch updateWith the same way to abort on `constructor` and `prototype`, but Y also rewrites the zipObjectDeep loop for no reason, iterating over `keys.length` and dropping the null-key guard, which risks changing behaviour.

X adds two nullish-coalescing guards that match the reference's behaviour (falsy non-nullish inputs give the same result either way), while Y rewrites the implementation signature, drops the defaults and adds an early return plus optional chaining, so its change is larger than needed and its bundle-size effect is less predictable.
